title: Following the historical paths of global communication
apa: Palmer, A. (2024). Following the historical paths of global communication. In Y. R. Kamalipour (Ed.), *Global communication: A multicultural perspective* (4th ed.). Rowman & Littlefield.
summary: Palmer opens the Kamalipour textbook with a long historical survey of how messages have crossed borders, from early writing systems, trade routes, and print to the telegraph, radio, satellites, and the internet. He treats each new medium as reorganizing who can speak across distance and on whose terms.
analysis: The chapter's central claim is that global communication has always followed the paths of trade, empire, and religion, so present day platforms inherit older routes rather than inventing new ones. Its method is synthetic narrative history, drawing on secondary sources to build a long timeline rather than testing a specific case. The contribution is orientation: it gives students a shared chronology that later readings such as Thussu and Mattelart complicate with political economy. Its main limit is a technology led storyline that tends to center Western inventions and European imperial networks, leaving non Western systems of exchange as background. Read beside Anderson, it supplies the infrastructure for print capitalism; for Eastern Europe, the same timeline can be reread through Habsburg, Ottoman, and Soviet communication networks that do not fit a simple Atlantic story.
note: Chapter 1 of the 4th edition (Rowman & Littlefield, March 2024), which matches the 2024 date; the same chapter title appears in the 2007 2nd edition. Page range not confirmed.

title: The origins of national consciousness
apa: Anderson, B. (2006). The origins of national consciousness. In *Imagined communities: Reflections on the origin and spread of nationalism* (Rev. ed., pp. 37-46). Verso. (Original work published 1983)
summary: Anderson argues that print capitalism made nations imaginable: publishers seeking larger markets standardized vernacular languages, and readers of the same books and newspapers came to picture themselves as a bounded community of strangers. The chapter explains why national consciousness emerged where and when it did.
analysis: The chapter locates the birth of the nation in a material convergence of capitalism, print technology, and linguistic diversity rather than in ancient ethnic essences. Its method is comparative historical sociology, moving quickly across European cases such as Luther's Reformation pamphlets and the decline of Latin. Its lasting contribution is to make media central to political identity, which is why every later reading on mediascapes and imagined worlds, including Appadurai, builds on it. A fair critique is that its account is European in origin and diffusionist, and later scholars such as Partha Chatterjee argue that anticolonial nationalisms were not simply copies of a European model. For Eastern Europe, the chapter is directly useful: the print languages of Czech, Polish, Hungarian, and the Baltic states were built through exactly this vernacular standardization, often against imperial languages like German and Russian.

title: Approaches to theorizing international communication
apa: Thussu, D. K. (2019). Approaches to theorizing international communication. In *International communication: Continuity and change* (3rd ed.). Bloomsbury Academic.
summary: Thussu surveys the main theoretical traditions used to study international communication, from modernization and development communication through dependency and cultural imperialism to globalization, cultural studies, and public sphere approaches. He sets them side by side so students can see what each explains and what it leaves out.
analysis: The chapter argues that no single paradigm captures international communication, and that political economy and cultural approaches need each other. Its method is a structured literature review organized by school, with short summaries of figures such as Lerner, Schramm, Schiller, and Hall. The contribution is a map of the field that the rest of the semester fills in with cases. Its limit is that the survey remains weighted toward Anglo American theory even while noting calls to internationalize media studies, a problem Thussu himself takes up in the 2022 article. For an Eastern Europe case, the chapter's Cold War modernization and propaganda frameworks are the obvious starting point, though they tend to treat the region as an object of Western and Soviet broadcasting rather than as a producer of theory.
note: Chapter 2 of the 3rd edition per the Bloomsbury table of contents. Chapter 1 is the historical context chapter; if the course file is historical, the assigned chapter may be ch. 1 instead.

title: De-colonizing global news-flows: A historical perspective
apa: Thussu, D. K. (2022). De-colonizing global news-flows: A historical perspective. *Journalism Studies, 23*(13), 1578-1592. https://doi.org/10.1080/1461670X.2022.2083007
summary: Thussu traces how the global news system grew out of empire, with agencies like Reuters built along imperial telegraph lines, and revisits the 1970s UNESCO fight over a New World Information and Communication Order. He argues that US digital platforms now reproduce a similar imbalance in a new form.
analysis: The core argument is continuity: the infrastructure and agenda setting power of global news have moved from colonial agencies to Western broadcasters to Silicon Valley platforms without breaking the pattern of Northern control. Evidence is historical and institutional, drawing on agency histories, UNESCO documents, and platform market data rather than new empirical fieldwork. Its contribution is to reconnect current talk of decolonizing media with the forgotten NWICO debates, giving the Global South a longer history of resistance. One limit is that framing platforms as neocolonial can flatten differences between platform power and territorial empire, and can underplay regional powers like China and Russia that also project news abroad. For Eastern Europe it raises a sharp question: the region was a site of Soviet counterflow in the NWICO era and is now a target of both Western platforms and Russian state media.
note: Open access status not confirmed; the Taylor & Francis page blocked automated checks.

title: Glocalising radio during empire
apa: Gadzekpo, A. (2018). Glocalising radio during empire. *Obsidian: Literature and Arts in the African Diaspora, 44*(2), 164-181.
summary: Gadzekpo examines colonial era radio in the Gold Coast, now Ghana, showing how a medium introduced to serve imperial administration was reshaped by local broadcasters, languages, and audiences. The essay appears in a special issue on radio and Ghanaian literature and broadcast culture.
analysis: The argument is that colonial radio was glocalised from the start: Ghanaian announcers, translators, and writers adapted British models to vernacular languages, local music, and local storytelling. The method is archival and biographical media history, informed by the author's related work on the pioneering broadcaster B. S. Gadzekpo. Its contribution is to move agency from London to Accra and to complicate the one way cultural imperialism model that Dorfman and Mattelart represent in the same week. A limit is that stressing local adaptation can soften the coercive frame of the colonial state, which still controlled licensing, content, and wartime propaganda. The piece offers a template for Eastern Europe as well, where Soviet and later Western international broadcasters were localized by national staff in ways that exceeded their sponsors' intentions.
note: Citation confirmed from the author's University of Ghana faculty page (Obsidian 44(2), pp. 164-181). No verified free copy found.

title: How to read Donald Duck: Imperialist ideology in the Disney comic
apa: Dorfman, A., & Mattelart, A. (2018). *How to read Donald Duck: Imperialist ideology in the Disney comic* (D. Kunzle, Trans.). OR Books. (Original work published 1971)
summary: Written in Allende's Chile, this study reads Disney comics as carriers of capitalist and imperialist values, from the treatment of money and work to the depiction of native peoples as childlike. It became the founding text of cultural imperialism critique.
analysis: Dorfman and Mattelart argue that seemingly innocent entertainment naturalizes consumerism and a colonial view of the Global South for young readers. Their method is ideological close reading of a large sample of Disney comics, combining Marxist and semiotic analysis. The book's importance is historical as much as analytical: it was banned and burned after the 1973 coup and helped define the Latin American school of communication research. Its main weakness, pressed later by Appadurai and audience researchers, is that it infers effects from texts and gives readers almost no capacity to resist or rework meaning. Set against Gadzekpo in the same week, it shows the two poles of the course, imposition and adaptation, and it invites comparison with Soviet era readings of Western popular culture in Eastern Europe.
note: Listed as discussed rather than assigned; the current OR Books English edition is used for the ISBN.

title: The culture factory; The power of propaganda
apa: Mattelart, A. (2000). *Networking the world, 1794-2000* (L. Carey-Libbrecht & J. A. Cohen, Trans.). University of Minnesota Press.
summary: Chapter 2 follows the rise of mass culture industries such as film, news agencies, and advertising as they became international businesses. Chapter 3 traces how states, especially during the world wars and the Cold War, turned these networks into instruments of propaganda.
analysis: Mattelart's argument is that the dream of universal communication has always been bound up with commerce and war, so networks sold as bringing humanity together also served markets and military strategy. His method is a genealogy of ideas and institutions, moving between engineers, entrepreneurs, and propagandists across two centuries. The contribution is to show that the culture industries and propaganda machines grew from the same infrastructure, which sets up the day's documentary on Pentagon influence in Hollywood. A limit is its breadth: the book compresses many national cases and still tells the story largely from French, British, and American archives. For Eastern Europe the propaganda chapter is directly relevant, since Radio Free Europe, Radio Liberty, and Soviet external broadcasting were central battlegrounds of the Cold War information war.
note: Chose Networking the World (2000) over Mapping World Communication (1994) because its chapters 2 and 3 are titled The culture factory and The power of propaganda, which match the paired documentary on military propaganda.

title: Theaters of war: How the Pentagon and CIA took Hollywood
apa: Stahl, R. (Director). (2022). *Theaters of war: How the Pentagon and CIA took Hollywood* [Film]. Media Education Foundation.
summary: This 87 minute documentary uses Freedom of Information Act documents to show how the US military and CIA shape Hollywood scripts in exchange for access to equipment, bases, and expertise. It covers productions from classic war films to superhero franchises.
analysis: Stahl's argument is that state security agencies act as uncredited script editors, removing war crimes, torture, and failures while promoting recruitment friendly narratives. The evidence is documentary: internal production notes and correspondence obtained through FOIA, paired with interviews with researchers and veterans. Its contribution is to give Mattelart's history of propaganda a contemporary, well sourced case and to show how soft power travels through global box office. A limit is its focus on US institutions, which leaves open how audiences abroad actually read these films and how other states run similar arrangements. For Eastern Europe, it invites comparison with Russian state funding of patriotic war cinema, a parallel system worth studying on its own terms.
note: Available to DU students on Kanopy; the link is the distributor's film page.

title: Globalization and culture
apa: Tomlinson, J. (1999). Globalization and culture. In *Globalization and culture*. Polity Press.
summary: Tomlinson defines globalization as complex connectivity, the dense web of interconnections in modern life, and argues that culture is both shaped by and constitutive of it. He separates connectivity from ideas of proximity and a single global culture, and distinguishes culture from communication technology.
analysis: The chapter's argument is that globalization lies at the heart of modern culture and cultural practice lies at the heart of globalization, without either being the master cause. Its method is conceptual clarification, correcting slippages in Harvey, Robertson, Ohmae, Hirst and Thompson, and Waters through vivid examples like the airline passenger and the Brent Spar campaign. Its lasting contribution is the insistence that most people experience globalization by staying in place while distant forces reshape their locality, which anticipates the streaming era. Critics such as Bergesen note that it treats connectivity as newer than it is and says little about ownership and power, a gap Appadurai's politics and the Netflix article partly fill. For Eastern Europe, the stay at home thesis fits populations who experienced 1989 and EU accession largely through media and markets arriving at home.
note: Page range omitted: the course file is a PDF scan without printed page numbers; add Polity pages if required.

title: Disjuncture and difference in the global cultural economy
apa: Appadurai, A. (1990). Disjuncture and difference in the global cultural economy. *Public Culture, 2*(2), 1-24. https://doi.org/10.1215/08992363-2-2-1
summary: Appadurai replaces center and periphery models with five overlapping flows, ethnoscapes, mediascapes, technoscapes, finanscapes, and ideoscapes, that move along disjunctive paths. He argues that the imagination is now a social practice through which people build imagined worlds from these flows.
analysis: The essay claims that the global cultural economy is organized by disjunctures between flows of people, machines, money, images, and ideas, so homogenization and heterogenization happen at once. Its method is theoretical and illustrative, drawing on fieldwork knowledge of Bombay, Gulf migration, and the Filipino taste for American pop. It gave media studies the scapes vocabulary and helped move the field from cultural imperialism toward indigenization and hybridity. Heyman and Campbell and political economists respond that the emphasis on flows underplays capital, borders, and unequal rights to move. The essay also names Russianization as a fear of the Baltic states and Armenia, which makes it a ready anchor for an Eastern Europe case built around a nearby dominant power rather than America.

title: The invisible doctrine: The secret history of neoliberalism
apa: Hutchison, P., & Sabian, L. (Directors). (2024). *The invisible doctrine: The secret history of neoliberalism* [Film]. Media Education Foundation.
summary: Built around the writing of George Monbiot, this 75 minute documentary traces neoliberalism from a 1930s fringe philosophy to the unnamed common sense of politics and economics. It links deregulation and privatization to inequality, weakened democracy, and environmental damage, and ends with proposals for participatory democracy and shared commons.
analysis: The film argues that neoliberalism's power comes partly from being invisible, spread through think tanks, business funded media, and policy networks until it seemed natural. Its evidence is a mix of archival footage, interviews, and Monbiot's narration, making it an argument essay on film rather than a neutral history. In the course it supplies the political economy behind the 1990s wave of media privatization that framed the Western Europe Netflix case. A limit is its advocacy tone and its focus on Anglo American actors, which leaves out how neoliberal reform was experienced elsewhere. Eastern Europe is a striking gap, since post 1989 shock therapy in Poland and Russia is among the clearest real world tests of the doctrine the film describes.
note: Directed by Peter Hutchison and Lucas Sabian with George Monbiot; cited under the directors per APA film format. Kanopy access through DU.

title: Culture as window dressing? A threefold methodological framework for researching the locality of Netflix series
apa: Idiz, D. R., Noordegraaf, J., & Vliegenthart, R. (2025). Culture as window dressing? A threefold methodological framework for researching the locality of Netflix series. *Critical Studies in Television, 20*(1), 93-117. https://doi.org/10.1177/17496020241235579
summary: The authors combine Top 10 industry data, close reading of five crime series, and coded audience reviews to test whether Netflix's European productions deliver local culture. They find that locality appears mainly as touristic backdrop and that reviewers rarely judge series on it.
analysis: The article argues that Netflix's European Originals are placed rather than place based: landmarks and topical themes signal locality while a transnational house style drives the storytelling. Its method is the threefold framework itself, linking catalogue data, textual analysis, and reception coding through a shared set of locality markers. The contribution is a replicable instrument for EU cultural policy debates, suggesting that content quotas count the wrong thing if culture is window dressing. Limits include a small textual sample, reliance on Netflix's own promotional data, and review sites that hide reviewer nationality, so locality is measured from the supply side. The framework transfers well to Eastern Europe, where Netflix's Polish Originals such as 1983 and The Border offer a test of whether a smaller market's locality survives the house style.
note: Open access (CC BY). The first author's initials are D. R. (Daphne Rena), not S.

title: Deterritorialization: The cultural condition of globalization
apa: Tomlinson, J. (1999). Deterritorialization: The cultural condition of globalization. In *Globalization and culture*. Polity Press.
summary: Tomlinson develops deterritorialization as the weakening tie between culture and place, lived through everyday media, food, shopping, and home life rather than dramatic travel. He answers objections about pre modern localism and unevenness and pairs the concept with reterritorialization and hybridity.
analysis: The chapter argues that globalization transforms locality rather than erasing it, producing an ambivalent mix of familiarity and difference, wider horizons and new vulnerabilities. Its method is phenomenological, working through Auge's non places, Williams's patriotic couple, global food, and Garcia Canclini's Tijuana. Its contribution is a vocabulary for the mundane globalization of people who never leave home, including the idea that anchoring identity to the nation now takes active work. Massey, quoted in the chapter, supplies the strongest critique: unevenness is not only about access but about who controls flows, and Tomlinson's reply keeps the affluent Western subject near the center. For Eastern Europe, the fall of the Berlin Wall appears in the chapter as a deterritorializing event, and post 1989 labor migration to the UK is a live example of reterritorialized communities.
note: Page range omitted: the course scan is cited by PDF page in her notes; add Polity pages if required.

title: A global sense of place
apa: Massey, D. (1994). A global sense of place. In *Space, place, and gender* (pp. 146-156). University of Minnesota Press.
summary: Massey asks whether a sense of place can be progressive and outward looking rather than defensive and nostalgic. She introduces the power geometry of time space compression and redefines places as meeting points of wider social relations, using her own Kilburn High Road as the example.
analysis: The essay's central move is to reject both the idea that globalization dissolves place and the reactionary defense of bounded, authentic communities. Its method is theoretical argument grounded in close observation of a London street, combined with pointed examples like the woman collecting water and Rio's favela residents. The power geometry concept is its lasting contribution, showing that some groups initiate flows, some receive them, and some are trapped by them. A limit is that the essay is short and programmatic, offering few tools for measuring power geometry empirically, and it still starts from a Western metropolitan vantage it criticizes. For Eastern Europe, it offers a way to read post 1989 nationalist heritage politics and migrant flows as struggles over who controls mobility rather than simple losses of authenticity.
note: Free link is the original 1991 Marxism Today version hosted by the Amiel and Melburn Trust archive; the course text is the 1994 book reprint, which is lightly revised.

title: Ethnography in/of the world system: The emergence of multi-sited ethnography
apa: Marcus, G. E. (1995). Ethnography in/of the world system: The emergence of multi-sited ethnography. *Annual Review of Anthropology, 24*, 95-117. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.an.24.100195.000523
summary: Marcus reviews an emerging style of ethnography that follows its object across multiple locations instead of staying in one village or site. He lays out six strategies for constructing such a field: follow the people, the thing, the metaphor, the plot or story, the life, and the conflict.
analysis: The article argues that the world system cannot be treated as mere context for a local study; it has to be traced through chains of connected sites. Its method is a review essay that organizes existing studies, from Malinowski to Emily Martin, into a typology of research designs. Its contribution is practical: it turns abstract globalization theory such as Appadurai's scapes into a method a researcher can actually use. Critics worry that multi sited work trades depth for breadth and that the researcher's own mobility, often a Western privilege, shapes which sites get followed. For an Eastern Europe media case, follow the thing or follow the conflict offers a clear design, for example tracing a Russian or Ukrainian news story across state television, Telegram channels, and diaspora audiences.
note: Course file is an excerpt (pp. 105-110) of the full article.

title: Media representation and the global imagination
apa: Orgad, S. (2012). *Media representation and the global imagination*. Polity Press.
summary: Orgad examines how news, advertising, television, and online media build our pictures of distant others and of our own place in the world. She organizes the book around five imaginative frames: the other, the nation, possible lives, the world, and the self.
analysis: Orgad argues that media representations are not just accurate or biased copies of reality but resources for a global imagination that shapes how people act toward distant others. Her method is critical synthesis across representation studies, using examples such as humanitarian appeals, migration coverage, and global advertising. The contribution is to join Appadurai's imagination as social practice with Hall's representation theory into a single framework for global media. A limit is that the book is mostly a conceptual map with limited original audience research, so the effects of representations on imagination are argued more than shown. It pairs naturally with the Sub Saharan Africa case and with Eastern Europe, where Western coverage long cast the region as grey, post Soviet, and in transition.
note: Author only on the syllabus; chose Shani Orgad's 2012 Polity book as the standard global media representation text. The specific chapter assigned is unknown.

title: Framing: Toward clarification of a fractured paradigm
apa: Entman, R. M. (1993). Framing: Toward clarification of a fractured paradigm. *Journal of Communication, 43*(4), 51-58. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1460-2466.1993.tb01304.x
summary: Entman offers a working definition of framing as selecting some aspects of reality and making them salient to promote a particular problem definition, causal interpretation, moral evaluation, and remedy. He argues the concept can unify scattered research across communication studies.
analysis: The essay's core claim is that framing is a shared paradigm hidden under inconsistent usage, and that clarifying it would link studies of texts, audiences, and power. Its method is conceptual, illustrated with short examples such as Cold War coverage that framed events through a US versus Soviet lens. Its four function definition became one of the most cited in the field and structures much later work on migration and conflict coverage. A limit is that it treats framing mainly as something done by journalists and elites to audiences, leaving less room for counter framing and, in a global setting, for non Western news systems. Paired with the Refugee Selfies episode, it sets up a contrast between how mainstream coverage frames migrants and how migrants frame themselves, a dynamic visible in Eastern European reporting on the 2015 Balkan route and the 2022 Ukrainian displacement.
note: Author only on the syllabus; chose the 1993 framing essay as the standard assignment. The alternative is Entman (2003) Cascading activation, Political Communication 20(4), if the week centers on foreign policy news.

title: Refugee selfies and the media of migration
apa: Llamas-Rodriguez, J. (Host). (2020, December 15). Refugee selfies and the media of migration (with Eszter Zimanyi) (Season 1, Episode 11) [Audio podcast episode]. In *Global media cultures*. Acast. https://shows.acast.com/global-media-cultures/episodes/refugee-selfies-and-the-media-of-migration
summary: Eszter Zimanyi discusses refugee selfies posted to Instagram during the 2015 European migration crisis, found through the platform's location tags. She reads them as digital transience, a way for migrants to mark presence in places they are passing through.
analysis: The episode argues that refugee selfies interrupt the dominant news frames of threat or victimhood by letting migrants author their own images of movement and place. Zimanyi's method is visual and platform analysis of public Instagram posts tied to geotagged locations along the route. The contribution is to shift attention from representation of refugees to self representation by refugees, and to show how platform features shape that possibility. A limit is that public selfies are a skewed sample of those with phones, connectivity, and safety to post, and platform visibility can also expose migrants to surveillance. Because the Balkan route runs through Hungary, Serbia, Croatia, and Slovenia, the episode maps directly onto Eastern Europe as a transit zone and onto the border politics of those states.
note: Matched on title: Global Media Cultures podcast, hosted by Juan Llamas-Rodriguez, the only podcast episode found with this title.

title: Mapping global media flow and contra-flow
apa: Thussu, D. K. (2007). Mapping global media flow and contra-flow. In D. K. Thussu (Ed.), *Media on the move: Global flow and contra-flow*. Routledge.
summary: Thussu maps the dominant flow of media from the United States and Europe alongside contra-flows from places such as India, Brazil, Mexico, Qatar, and China. He distinguishes transnational contra-flows with global reach from geo-cultural ones serving regional and diaspora audiences.
analysis: The chapter argues that US dominance persists but is no longer total, as Bollywood, telenovelas, Al Jazeera, and Asian television build audiences beyond their home markets. The method is descriptive political economy using industry revenues, audience reach, and corporate histories. Its contribution is the flow and contra-flow vocabulary, which gives the cultural imperialism debate a more plural map without dropping power. A limit is that contra-flows are often small, commercially driven, and sometimes state sponsored, so they may mirror rather than challenge the dominant model, a point Thussu concedes. For Eastern Europe the framework raises the case of Russia Today as a state funded contra-flow and of Polish and Czech streaming exports as smaller geo-cultural flows.
note: Chose Thussu's opening chapter in his edited volume Media on the Move (Routledge, 2007 per the syllabus; some catalogs list 2006). Page range not confirmed.

title: In the meantime: Temporality and cultural politics
apa: Sharma, S. (2014). *In the meantime: Temporality and cultural politics*. Duke University Press.
summary: Sharma studies how different groups live time under global capitalism, from frequent flyers and taxi drivers to office workers and slow living advocates. She argues that speed is not experienced equally and that some people's time is maintained by others' labor.
analysis: The book's central claim is that time, like Massey's space, has a power geometry: the jet lagged executive's temporal comfort depends on drivers, cleaners, and service workers whose time is shaped around it. Sharma's method mixes ethnography, interviews, and cultural analysis of airports, taxis, yoga at work, and slow movements. The contribution is a temporal politics of globalization that corrects celebratory accounts of speed and connectivity, including Tomlinson's culture of speed. A limit is its concentration on North American settings, which leaves open how temporal inequality looks in the Global South. If this is the assigned Sharma, it connects directly to Polson's work on privileged mobility and offers Eastern Europe a lens on migrant care and transport labor that sustains Western European time.
note: Author only on the syllabus and the course week is a midterm quiz day. Chose Sarah Sharma's In the Meantime because it extends Massey's power geometry and fits Polson's research on mobility; could also be a different Sharma text on globalization. Confirm against the syllabus.

title: Digital diasporas: Beyond the buzzword. Toward a relational understanding of mobility and connectivity
apa: Candidatu, L., Leurs, K., & Ponzanesi, S. (2019). Digital diasporas: Beyond the buzzword. Toward a relational understanding of mobility and connectivity. In J. Retis & R. Tsagarousianou (Eds.), *The handbook of diasporas, media, and culture* (pp. 31-47). Wiley.
summary: The authors review three waves of research on diasporas online, from cyberculture to ethnography to data driven studies, and propose a relational approach grounded in feminist and postcolonial theory. They draw on Glissant's ideas of relation and creolization to move beyond fixed origins.
analysis: The chapter argues that digital diaspora has become a buzzword that hides power, treating migrants either as isolated or as celebrated cosmopolitans. Its method is a critical literature review that reads each research paradigm for what it can and cannot see. The contribution is a relational framework that treats online and offline, continuity and change, and multiple axes of inequality as entangled. A limit is that the chapter is programmatic and offers few worked cases, so the framework's practical payoff is left to later studies. For Eastern Europe, it gives a better way to study Romanian, Polish, and Ukrainian diasporas in Western Europe, whose messaging groups and media habits cross national lines in ways a simple homeland versus host model misses.
note: Chose the 2019 handbook chapter; the free copy is the authors' accepted version in the Utrecht University repository.

title: Introduction: Mapping global digital cultures
apa: Punathambekar, A., & Mohan, S. (2019). Introduction: Mapping global digital cultures. In A. Punathambekar & S. Mohan (Eds.), *Global digital cultures: Perspectives from South Asia* (pp. 1-35). University of Michigan Press. https://doi.org/10.3998/mpub.9561751
summary: The editors argue that digital cultures in South Asia should be studied as central to global transformations rather than as local variants of Silicon Valley models. They organize the field around infrastructures, platforms, and publics.
analysis: The introduction claims that global internet studies has been provincial, generalizing from US and European cases, and that South Asia reveals different relations among states, markets, and media. Its method is a framing essay that synthesizes regional scholarship and previews the volume's chapters. The contribution is the infrastructures, platforms, and publics triad, which gives students a portable way to analyze any region's digital culture. A limit is the tension between de-Westernizing and still using categories developed largely in Western platform studies. The triad works well for the Eastern Europe case, for example Estonia's e-state infrastructure, Russia's VK and Yandex platforms, and Ukrainian wartime publics on Telegram.
note: Chose the open access introduction to their 2019 edited volume; the week pairs it with the China case, so a specific chapter may be assigned instead.

title: Algorithmic cosmopolitanism: On the global claims of digital entertainment platforms
apa: Elkins, E. (2019). Algorithmic cosmopolitanism: On the global claims of digital entertainment platforms. *Critical Studies in Media Communication, 36*(4), 376-389.
summary: Elkins examines how Netflix and similar platforms describe their recommendation systems as bringing a borderless, cosmopolitan culture to viewers everywhere. He shows how that rhetoric sits alongside geoblocking, uneven catalogues, and corporate strategy.
analysis: The argument is that algorithmic cosmopolitanism is a corporate discourse that presents personalized taste communities as replacing national audiences while serving market expansion. Elkins's method is critical discourse analysis of executive statements, press materials, and platform design, informed by his research on regional lockout. The contribution is to name how platforms claim a universal, post national identity while still enforcing borders through licensing and geoblocking. A limit is that the analysis centers on company rhetoric more than on how viewers in different markets actually use recommendations. It connects directly to Idiz et al. and to Eastern Europe, where catalogue gaps and later entry of Netflix left many viewers with a thinner version of the promised global library.
note: Author only on the syllabus; chose the 2019 article over his book Locked Out (NYU Press, 2019). DOI not verified, so doi_url is left null.

title: Digitality and debordered spaces in the era of streaming: A Global South perspective
apa: Khalil, J. F., & Zayani, M. (2022). Digitality and debordered spaces in the era of streaming: A Global South perspective. *Television & New Media, 23*(2), 167-183. https://doi.org/10.1177/15274764211014584
summary: Using Saskia Sassen's idea of third spaces, the authors study Shahid, the Arab streaming platform run by MBC Group. They argue that such services work inside national regulation while also reaching across borders, creating new sites for regional cultural politics.
analysis: The article claims that Global South streaming platforms are neither simple local answers to Netflix nor extensions of the state, but debordered spaces that operate at several scales at once. The method is a qualitative case study of Shahid's business model, content strategy, and regulatory setting, framed by Sassen's theory of globalization. Its contribution is to move the platform debate beyond Silicon Valley and show regional players reshaping flows. A limit is dependence on a single firm tied to Saudi capital, which makes it hard to separate platform logic from state influence. For Eastern Europe it offers a template for studying regional platforms such as Poland's Player or Russia's Kinopoisk, which also balance national rules against transnational audiences.
note: Author pair only on the syllabus. Chose their 2022 Television & New Media article; an alternative is their open access chapter Streaming the Middle East: From legacy media to digital platforms (2023) in Digital Platforms and the Global South (Routledge). Confirm against the syllabus.

title: Eastern Europe regional case study (reading TBD)
note: Stacy's own regional case; reading to be chosen.

title: State
apa: Crawford, K. (2021). State. In *Atlas of AI: Power, politics, and the planetary costs of artificial intelligence*. Yale University Press.
summary: In the chapter on the state, Crawford follows how AI systems developed for military and intelligence purposes, such as those exposed in the Snowden files, move into policing, border control, and municipal government. She shows how state and corporate surveillance have merged.
analysis: Crawford's argument across the book is that AI is an extractive industry of minerals, labor, and data, and this chapter shows the state as both its sponsor and its customer. Her method is investigative and archival, tracing contracts, leaked documents, and vendors like Palantir across agencies. The contribution is to treat AI as infrastructure of state power rather than as neutral technology, which fits the day's pairing with Helberg. A limit is that the chapter is anchored in the US and UK security state, with less attention to how authoritarian states build their own systems. For the Russia and Eurasia case, it provides a lens for comparing Western surveillance capitalism with Russia's SORM monitoring system and Moscow's facial recognition network.

title: The wires of war: Technology and the global struggle for power
apa: Helberg, J. (2021). *The wires of war: Technology and the global struggle for power*. Avid Reader Press.
summary: Helberg, a former Google policy lead on disinformation, describes a technological cold war between democracies and the authoritarian regimes of China and Russia. He divides it into a front end fight over platforms and information and a back end fight over 5G, chips, and cables.
analysis: The book argues that control of digital infrastructure and information space is now the main arena of great power competition and that the United States is losing ground. Its method is a policy insider's narrative built on interviews, case studies of Russian interference and Chinese technology firms, and his own time at Google. The contribution for this course is to show how a Washington security perspective frames global media as a battlefield. Its main limit is that framing, which treats US platforms as defenders of democracy and largely brackets their own power and extraction, the problem Crawford and Thussu raise. For Russia and Eurasia, and for Stacy's Eastern Europe region, it is a useful primary source on how Russian disinformation in Ukraine, the Baltics, and elections is understood in US policy circles.
note: ISBN is the 2022 paperback; the original hardcover appeared in 2021.
